en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui, Part Four:
Refuting the Aggregate of Mental Formations (saṃskāra-skandha). Section Three: One, the characteristics of the exhausted and the unexhausted, in two parts: One, clarifying the scope, in two parts:
One, the characteristic of the benefit of the exhaustion of perception (saṃjñā).

"Ānanda! When those sons of good family who cultivate samādhi have exhausted the aggregate of perception, their ordinary dreams and fantasies will vanish, and they will remain constant and unified whether awake or asleep."
"If the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) persists, then upon waking one immediately forms mental images, and while asleep it becomes a dream.
Now that the aggregate of perception has been exhausted, there are no longer any dreams, because the aggregate of perception is the very source of dreams."

Regarding "awakening and sleep being one": although there are states of awakening and sleep, because they are without conceptualization, awakening is like sleep and sleep is like awakening; therefore, it is said that they are eternally one.
"The awakened clarity is empty and still, like a clear sky; there are no longer any coarse, heavy shadows of external objects.
The perfectly luminous essence of the mind is called "awakened clarity."
Because one is free from the fluctuations of thought, it is called "empty stillness.

"Empty" is a metaphor for awakened clarity; "clear weather" is a metaphor for being free from thought; and "coarseness" refers to afflictions, because the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is the turbidity of affliction.
The shadows and phenomena of external objects are precisely the realms of what is conceptualized.
Since the conceptualizing subject has vanished, the conceptualized object cannot be established; therefore, it is said that they no longer exist.

Observe all the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers: they are like a bright mirror, to which things coming do not adhere and things passing leave no trace, receiving reflections and responses in emptiness.

"Contemplation is the condition; although the faculties and consciousnesses take various objects as conditions, one does not form mental images or fixate thoughts upon them. Thus, like a mirror reflecting objects without leaving a trace, it merely receives, reflects, and responds in emptiness."
It may also be like a mirror reflecting light; although it discerns, there is no shadow, and thus it is said to "receive in emptiness.
It is utterly devoid of habitual tendencies, being solely pure and true.
"Liǎo" (了) means "ultimately.
"Wǎng" (罔) means "non-existent.
"Chén" (陳) means "ancient."
"Habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) are deluded conceptualizations.
Ultimately, there is no such thing as beginningless deluded habituation; there is only the single, spiritual nature of true thusness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, "to cognize" (*vijñapti*) means to discern, which refers to the various consciousnesses.
"Entanglement" refers to the phantom-like mental image (*māyā*).
"Habitual patterns" refers to the seeds from time immemorial.
"The sole, subtle, and true" refers to the single aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

As the subsequent text states: "Then, the profound clarity is internally devoid of form, empty and non-existent. Because subtle and refined contemplation is used to counteract the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), it is called "refined truth" (*jingzhen*).

This reveals that the practitioner has attained the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), leaving only the aggregates of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) and formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
Now, this aggregate of formations is further revealed and disclosed; therefore, the aggregate of consciousness is termed the "pure essence" (jingzhen).
2. The Manifestation of the Aggregate of Formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

"The root-source of arising and ceasing is here revealed, such that all twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions are fully disclosed. Although their individual life-threads have not yet been penetrated, their common basis of birth is seen, shimmering and turbid like a mirage; it serves as the ultimate pivot-hole for the floating sense-faculties and their objects. This is called the domain of the aggregate of formations."
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the source of arising and ceasing, because it involves constant flux and volitional activity.
Since formations manifest when perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are exhausted, it is said that they are "revealed.

Regarding the phrase "exhausting their categories": *dan* means "to exhaust" or "to finish. This means that all twelve classes of living beings emerge from formations, because formations constitute the essence of karma.

Regarding "those who have not yet attained penetration each receive their own life-force": although they already understand that the twelve classes of beings all emerge from mental formations (*saṃskāra*), they do not yet know that the distinct seeds of sentient beings reside within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). These are precisely the seeds of karma and suffering within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which constitute the primary cause and the ultimate source for the individual life-force of each sentient being.

"Seeing the basis of co-arising" refers to the basis of the homogeneous class (*sabhāga*), which is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); the twelve categories all take this aggregate of formations as their fundamental basis.
"It is like a mirage" means that when dust combines with the yang energy, it is stirred up and manifested.
"Brilliantly shimmering" refers to the arising and flickering of light, which serves as a metaphor for birth and cessation.

"Pure agitation" refers to the turbulence of this *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), where birth and cessation occur in a subtle, incessant manner; it is called "pure" because it is free from the defilements of the *asaṃjñika-skandha* (the aggregate of non-perception).

Regarding "the ultimate pivot and socket for the floating faculties and sense-objects": the pivot is the hinge of a door, and the socket is the mortise of a door; these are both the essential points of movement and rotation.

The faculties and objects, as well as birth and cessation, all take the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as their mechanical fulcrum. To thoroughly understand this lies precisely within the *skandha* of formations; therefore, it is called the "domain" (*qūyǔ*).
2. Clarifying the characteristic of exhaustion:

"If this turbid and flickering primordial nature enters into the primordial clarity of its own nature, and once clarified, its primordial habituation ceases—like waves subsiding and transforming into still water—this is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations)."
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings; by observing its origins, one finds that hidden, subtle delusions constitute its root.

Regarding "the nature entering the primordial clarity": when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the nature of flux becomes clear and returns to the single storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*); this is called "entering the primordial clarity."
The Sūtra says, "The ocean of the storehouse consciousness abides eternally.

Through the increasing excellence of contemplative practice, one is able to cause the habitual energies of the root of pure arising-and-ceasing to become immovable, returning them to the single aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), just like water that has been clarified.
Because this is the nature of the karma of the transmigration of sentient beings, when it is exhausted, one transcends the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
The arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is subtle and difficult to perceive; therefore, it is called "profoundly hidden."
II. Correctly elucidating the manifest objects, in ten parts:
I. The two theories of causelessness, in two parts: A. The heading.

“Ānanda, you should know that when these good sons who have attained right awareness abide in *śamatha*, their minds are concentrated, luminous, and upright; thus, the ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity to harm them.”

Only then can one achieve refined study and exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings. Within that fundamental class of beings, when the primal source of life is revealed, one contemplates its profound clarity and its circular, agitated movement. If, within this circular source, one gives rise to conceptual calculations, such a person falls into the two theories of causelessness.
Because śamatha and vipaśyanā have increased and excelled, and discursive thoughts do not arise, it is said that "doubt is clarified and the right mind is established.
Because the defilement of craving in the desire realm does not arise, it is said that "Māra finds no opportunity."

In investigating the fundamental nature of sentient beings here, one finds that only the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)—subtle, hidden, pure, and void—is considered the source of all arising and ceasing.

Now that this has been revealed, there is nothing else outside of it that serves as the basis for sentient beings; yet, because they do not know that the causes and conditions of good and evil, as well as the seeds of differentiation, reside within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), they instead cling to the notion that the world arises without cause.

Thus, the treatises of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) arose from this; they all practiced until reaching this point, where false wisdom suddenly arose, which is called the "arising of views. It is not that there were originally separate non-Buddhist paths existing apart from this.
2. Explanation, in two parts: A.
Calculating that there is no original cause, in two parts:
1. The actual analysis.
"First, this person perceives that there is originally no cause. Why is this?

Because this person has already completely shattered the foundation of birth and, by means of the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty, sees the karmic currents of all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas—winding and circling as they die here and are born there—perceiving only the cycle of rebirth of these beings within those very places."
Beyond eighty thousand kalpas, there is a darkness in which nothing can be perceived; they then form this understanding:
"These sentient beings of the ten directions in this world have existed spontaneously for eighty thousand kalpas, without cause."
When the foundation of birth is completely shattered, the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) manifests.
The "eight hundred merits" refers to the fundamental portion of the eye-faculty being activated through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), becoming a hundredfold more excellent.
Riding upon this supernormal power, one perceives the deaths and births of sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas;

beyond this point, one no longer knows, for this is the limit where the power of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is exhausted. One does not yet know the cause for the arising of the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness), nor the distinctions in the ripening of fruits as conditioned by the seeds of *avidyā* (ignorance).

Because they do not understand this, they cling to the notion that things exist without an original cause; it is like seeing a flying bird at a distance beyond one's reach and concluding that it does not exist.
The sensory faculty of the eye can grasp objects only up to eight hundred *yojanas*, and worldly supernormal powers do not exceed this limit;
however, supramundane supernormal powers transcend this without obstruction.
2. Conclusion:
"By means of this conceptualization, one loses right and universal knowledge, falls into the ranks of external paths, and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
As the text says.
2. Calculating that the end has no cause, in two parts:
1. The formal analysis.
"Second, this person perceives that the end has no cause."

Why is this? Because these people have already perceived the root of birth; they know that humans give birth to humans and realize that birds give birth to birds. They see that crows have been black from the beginning and cranes have been white from the beginning; that humans and devas are fundamentally upright while animals are fundamentally horizontal. That whiteness is not produced by washing and blackness is not created by dyeing; that from eighty thousand kalpas ago there has been no further change or shift, and even now, at the end of this physical form, it remains exactly thus.
Since I have from the beginning never perceived bodhi, how could there be any further matter of attaining bodhi?
You should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause.
The first two phrases constitute the heading; what follows below provides the reason for this. Now, from here on, the text correctly elucidates the meaning that the derivative has no cause.
Because the fundamental has no cause, the derivative is likewise so.
One does not perceive Bodhi eighty thousand kalpas prior, nor is it any different eighty thousand kalpas thereafter.
Because one perceives that the root is non-existent, the branches are likewise non-existent.
Those who know that "a human gives birth to a human" understand that a human only gives birth to a human; there is no cause for a human to give birth to a bird.
"Only birds give birth to birds; there is no cause for humans to be born [from them].
This is because they do not understand that newly created distinct karma brings about rebirth in different species;
thus, they form this attachment. Second, the conclusion.
"By means of such speculative reckoning, one loses right and universal knowledge, falls into the ranks of external paths, and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the first type of external path that establishes the doctrine of causelessness."
2. The fourfold doctrine of eternalism has three parts:
first, the heading:
“Ānanda!...”
Among these good sons within this samādhi, their minds are concentrated, luminous, and upright, so that Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally restless source. Those who give rise to conceptual calculations within this perfect and eternal reality fall into the four theories of universal permanence.

Regarding "permanence and pervasiveness": because the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) continues in succession without interruption, it is called "permanent.
Because one reckons these four aspects as pervading all phenomena, it is called "pervasive."
2. Explanation, in four parts:
1. Constant for twenty thousand kalpas.

"First, this person exhausts the nature of the mind and its objects; finding no cause within these two realms, they cultivate the ability to know all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions during twenty thousand kalpas. Seeing that these all circulate in a cycle and have never been lost, they reckon this to be permanent."

Within this supreme meditative concentration, one takes both mind and its objects as the domain to be investigated. Through the perfection of this contemplation, one knows that throughout twenty thousand kalpas, the birth and death of sentient beings in the ten directions circulate in a cycle without ever being lost; they are like water becoming ice and ice returning to water—though they circulate, their essence is not lost, and thus they are called "constant."
2. "The second is 'eternity for forty thousand kalpas.

This person investigates the ultimate source of the four great elements and the eternal nature of the four characteristics; through cultivation, they are able to know that throughout forty thousand kalpas, all births and deaths of sentient beings in the ten directions are fundamentally constant and have never been lost, and thus they reckon them to be eternal."

This person, within their contemplation, takes the four great elements as the object of observation; once the contemplation is perfected, they are able to know the arising and ceasing of sentient beings throughout forty thousand kalpas, all of whom possess an eternally abiding essence.
Because all sentient beings take the four great elements as their substance, and since these four great elements are eternal, sentient beings are also eternal; therefore, they do not perish.
Third, they are eternal for eighty thousand kalpas.

"Third, this person exhausts the six sense faculties and reaches the fundamental source within the *manas*, the *ālayavijñāna*, and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because their nature is eternally constant. Through cultivation, they are able to know that all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas circulate without losing [their essence], being fundamentally and eternally abiding; they find that this nature is never lost, and thus they reckon it to be permanent."
In Sanskrit it is called *kliṣṭamanas*, which here means the "defiled mind.
As for "appropriation," this refers to the eighth consciousness.

By thoroughly investigating the nature of these eight consciousnesses, one finds that they are fundamentally eternal; because of this, one is able to know the arising and ceasing of sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas, as being neither interrupted nor dispersed.

Because all sentient beings are without exception possessed of the eight consciousnesses, and since these eight consciousnesses arise and perish without being lost, sentient beings are likewise so; therefore, they are called "constant."
4. Permanence through Non-arising and Non-ceasing.

"Fourth, once this person has exhausted the source of ideation, the principle of their nature no longer undergoes flowing, ceasing, or movement; since the mind of arising and ceasing has now been eternally extinguished, non-arising and non-ceasing naturally manifests within that principle."
"Because of what the mind has measured and transcended, one reckons it to be permanent.

The principle of arising is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Since one perceives that perception (*saṃjñā*) has ceased—and because perception is that which can move, and now it has already stilled—movement is no longer present; thus, the natural principle of non-arising and non-ceasing is itself the aggregate of formations.
This involves calculating non-arising and non-ceasing within what is subject to arising and ceasing; therefore, one clings to it as being permanent.
Third, the conclusion:
"Because of this calculation of permanence, one loses right and universal knowledge, falls into the ranks of external paths, and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi."
"This is what is called the second heterodox school’s doctrine of the perfect and eternal.
True Universal Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) is the very nature of Bodhi.

Because they engage in inverted discrimination, they lose this true knowledge; because they restrict it to only two, four, or eighty thousand kalpas and cannot know beyond that, they lose true universal knowledge."
Since the Omniscient One has passed away, these have thus become the heterodox arguments of non-Buddhists.
Third, the four types of "partially eternalist" theories (ekadeśa-śāśvata-vāda), in three parts:
first, the heading.
"Furthermore, among those sons of good family within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māras find no opportunity.
They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source."
Those who engage in conceptual speculation regarding self and others fall into the four inverted views and the doctrine that "one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.
Alternatively, they may cling to the notion that the self can produce others, asserting that the self is eternal while others are impermanent.
Or, some maintain that the self is produced from another, such that the other is eternal while the self is impermanent;
these all calculate that one part is impermanent and one part is eternal.
Second, the explanation has four parts:
1. "I am eternal, while that is impermanent.

First, this person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, profound and still, and takes it to be the ultimate divine self (*ātman*). From this, they calculate that the self pervades the ten directions, concentrated and luminous, unmoving; that all sentient beings are born and die within the center of their own mind. Thus, they name their own mind-nature "eternal," while those things subject to birth and death are truly of an impermanent nature.

This person, having practiced meditative concentration but not yet realized the Truth, observes within their tainted contemplation that the wondrous, luminous mind pervades the ten directions of the world. Seeing this through conceptualization, they fail to recognize that it is the illusory consciousness of ignorance manifesting shadows that appear as real. Clinging to this deluded mind as pervading the ten directions, they take it to be a true self—congealed, luminous, and immovable.
By virtue of being sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one perceives all sentient beings being born and dying within one's own mind; this is impermanence (*anitya*).
That which is unmoving within me is permanence (*nitya*).
Second, regarding the destruction and non-destruction of kalpas:

"Second, this person does not contemplate their own mind, but contemplates throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Where they see a kalpa being destroyed, they call it the ultimate nature of impermanence; where they see a kalpa not being destroyed, they call it the ultimate permanence."

This person, while in meditative absorption, uses supernormal powers to perceive the worlds of the ten directions; therein, seeing a world that has not yet disintegrated, they grasp it as permanent, and seeing a place where it has already disintegrated, they grasp it as having the nature of impermanence.
Although this involves observing the environment, it necessarily includes the primary retribution.
Third, "I am like a mote of dust that revolves.

Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being so subtle, fine, and dense that it is like a mote of dust; it transmigrates through the ten directions without its nature changing or altering, yet it can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant.
That which is indestructible in nature is called the self-nature of permanence;
that all birth and death flow forth from this self is called the nature of impermanence.

As for the statement "my mind is like a mote of dust," it is because the nature of the mind is subtle and secret, difficult to perceive, and thus likened to a mote of dust; it does not mean that it is small.
This [view] clings to the subtle nature of the mind and takes it to be the self (*ātman*).

"Self" means that which is autonomous and sovereign; thus, while its nature remains immutable and does not undergo change, it is capable of causing this coarse aggregate of the physical body to arise and perish.
Because these coarse aggregates all flow forth from my mind, that which flows forth is called impermanent, while that which is able to flow forth is called the nature of permanence.
Fourth, "conditioning factors are permanent while the rest are impermanent.
Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception has been exhausted and perceives the flow of the aggregate of conditioning factors (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

They reckon the constant flow of the aggregate of conditioning factors to be a permanent nature, whereas they name the fact that form, sensation, perception, and so forth have now been extinguished as impermanence.
Because the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is revealed as manifesting in a state of constant flux, one clings to it as permanent;
yet because it is temporarily suppressed and does not arise during the contemplation of perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other aggregates, one clings to it as impermanent.
Therefore, this body is partially impermanent and partially permanent.
Third, the conclusion:
"Because of such deliberations that [the body] is partially impermanent and partially permanent, one falls into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi."
This is called the third heterodox doctrine: the partial eternalism theory.
Fourth, the four theories of finitude, which consist of three parts:
first, the heading.
"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who maintain a firm, concentrated, and upright mind, Māras find no opportunity.

When they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, if they engage in conceptual calculations regarding its various states, such persons fall into the four theories of finitude."
In the sphere where the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, there are four stages; calculating these, one considers them as finite or infinite.
Second, the explanation has four parts:
first, the three periods of time.

"First, this person's mind calculates that the source of birth flows and functions without ceasing; calculating the past and future is called 'having limits,' while calculating the continuous mind is called 'being limitless.'"
"In this person, the mental calculations of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) flow and stream on in the present without ceasing; this is called 'boundless.
That which does not see the past or the future is called 'having limits.'"
This refers to the fact that because the flow of arising and ceasing never ceases and has no limit, it is called "boundless.
Second, regarding sentient beings:

"Second, when this person observes eighty thousand kalpas, they see sentient beings; prior to eighty thousand kalpas, there is silence with nothing heard or seen. That place where there is nothing heard or seen is called 'boundless,' while the place where there are sentient beings is called 'bounded.'"
"Although one may perceive sentient beings for eighty thousand kalpas, because there is still a limit to what is perceived, it is said to be finite.
Beyond this, where one perceives no further arising and thus no limit, one clings to the notion that it is infinite."
3. The Nature of the Mind.

"Third, this person conceives that they possess universal knowledge and have attained boundless nature; thus, all people appear within the scope of their own cognition. Yet, they claim they have never known the cognitive nature of those others, thereby asserting that those others do not possess a boundless mind, but rather possess a limited nature."
"I am able to fully know all sentient beings; because all sentient beings are currently known by me, I have attained the boundless mind.
As for those below me, although they possess knowledge, this knowledge does not manifest within my own knowledge. Because it does not manifest, it is therefore limited."
4. Arising and Ceasing.

"Fourth, this person exhausts the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and, based on what he perceives, employs the pathways of his mind to deliberate upon all sentient beings. Within a single body, he calculates that they are all half-arisen and half-ceased; he clarifies that within all worlds, one half has limits and one half is limitless."

Regarding the thorough investigation of the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): when ideation is exhausted, formations are laid bare; now, within this contemplation, one investigates them to realize their emptiness.

By investigating and thoroughly analyzing the mental calculations of the aggregate of formations, one sees that within the single body of every sentient being, things arise and perish in every instant, and the world is likewise so.
The place of birth has limits, while the place of cessation is limitless; this is because birth is perceptible to the senses, whereas cessation is not.
Third, the conclusion:
"By means of such deliberations regarding finitude and infinitude, one falls into the ranks of external paths and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi."
This is called the fourth heterodox doctrine established by those who maintain the theory of finitude.
Fifth, the four types of evasive speech regarding immortality, which are threefold:
first, the heading.
"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who maintain a firm, concentrated, and upright mind, Māras cannot find an opportunity.

As they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, if they give rise to conceptual calculations within their knowledge and views, such persons will fall into four kinds of inverted, 'immortal' equivocation—pervasive, false speculations."
This person is unable to make a definitive resolution regarding knowledge and vision; when questioned by others, they always give evasive and confused answers.

Regarding those who claim "immortality," according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, non-Buddhists reckon that the eternal nature of heaven is "immortality," and they maintain that by giving non-confused answers, one attains birth in that heaven.
If one were to answer immediately despite not truly knowing, there is a fear that it would constitute evasive equivocation (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
Therefore, when questioned, one might reply that it is secret and should not be disclosed, or provide an indefinite answer.
The Buddha’s Dharma rebukes this, saying: "This is truly evasive and confused.
Second, the explanation, in four parts:
first, the eightfold [analysis].
"First, this person contemplates the source of transformation: where they perceive shifting flow, they name it 'change'; where they perceive continuity, they name it 'permanence.
Where they perceive that which is seen, they name it 'arising'; where they do not perceive the place of seeing, they name it 'cessation.'"
The state in which the causal nature of continuity is uninterrupted is called "increase"; the point within that very continuity where it is severed is called "decrease.
The place where each [phenomenon] arises is called "existence," and the place where they mutually cease is called "non-existence."
"By means of principle one observes as a whole; by means of the mind one observes with particularity. "Observing with particularity" refers to the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Within the single process of arising and ceasing that constitutes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one distinguishes eight meanings; these particular observations consist of constancy and change, arising and ceasing, increase and decrease, and existence and non-existence.
"Not seeing the seer" means seeing non-seeing, because the locus of cessation cannot be seen.
The rest is as stated in the text.
"When a person seeking the Dharma comes and asks about its meaning, he answers: "
"I am now both arising and ceasing, both existent and non-existent, both increasing and decreasing.
At all times he thus confused his speech, causing the person before him to lose the sequence of the verses.
This response, which answers the question by summarizing the essential meaning, briefly cites six points.
Because it cannot definitively establish the underlying principle and instead provides a dualistic answer, it states that "it both arises and ceases," and so forth.
This causes the person before them to fail to grasp the meaning within the chapters and verses; therefore, it is said that they have "lost the chapters and verses.
Second, "only non-existence":
"Second, this person contemplates their mind and sees that it has no mutual location; because of this non-existence, they attain realization."
When someone comes to question him, he answers with only a single word, saying merely "non-existence" (*wu*); apart from this non-existence, there is nothing further he can say.
At the point where every thought-moment ceases, it is called mutual non-existence; for as soon as the mind arises, it immediately perishes, and no substantial entity can be found.
Since practice is thus, all dharmas are likewise; therefore, it is said that "one realizes through non-attainment.
Thus, when someone asks a question, one simply answers with "no.
Third, it is merely this.
"Third, this person carefully observes that the mind each has its own location, and through this, they attain realization.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying merely 'It is so'; other than this, they have nothing further to say."
In every moment of thought as it arises, each has its own name; based on this, one realizes that all things exist.

When someone comes to ask a question and one simply answers "yes," although one sees that the mind has arising in every moment and intends for all things to exist, and furthermore observes their cessation, one does not dare answer "they exist. Therefore, one simply answers "yes" to prevent such an error.
4. The View of Both Existence and Non-existence.
"The fourth is the view that people hold both existence and non-existence; because its object is bifurcated, the mind is likewise distracted.

When someone comes to question them, they answer that what is 'also existent' is precisely 'also non-existent,' and that within 'also non-existence' there is not 'also existence. This is entirely evasive and confused, allowing no room for further inquiry."
This refers to the dualistic conception of both existence and non-existence.
As for the statement that "because its object is manifold, the mind is also distracted," it is because the object is not fixed upon a single meaning that distraction arises.
The two previous treatises only partially established existence and non-existence respectively; this present treatise, however, perceives both existence and non-existence simultaneously.

As for the statement that "that which exists is also non-existent," the meaning is that within the very state of existence, there is non-existence, thereby establishing the conceptualization of both existence and non-existence.

"Nor is it that 'being neither' means it is not 'also being'" means that although one speaks of "non-existence" within "existence," the two characteristics are distinct; therefore, it is said that it is not "also being.
Regarding "there is no room for further interrogation": if one interrogates "existence" as being "non-existence," yet it is also said that "within non-existence it is not also being";
if one interrogates "non-existence" as not being "existence," yet it is also said that "being also" is precisely "being also non-existent."
Because they mutually obstruct and defend one another, it is difficult to interrogate them thoroughly.
Third, the conclusion:
"Due to these speculative calculations, which are deceptive, confused, and empty, they fall into the ways of external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi."
"This is what is called the fifth heterodox school: the pervasive, false discourse of the four inverted natures of 'immortality' and 'evasive equivocation.
Regarding these four doctrines, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: 'First, if śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others hold such a view as saying: "I do not know whether there is retribution for good and evil."'"
If asked such a question of me, I would not be able to answer.
Feeling shame and apprehension, I would have to reply:
"This matter is different; this matter is not different; this matter is neither different nor not different"—this constitutes the first view.
Second, when questioned regarding the existence or non-existence of future lives, he likewise gives this same answer.
Third, when questioned as to what constitutes good or evil, he likewise gives this same answer.
Fourth, being ignorant, dull-witted, and obtuse, if others question him, he simply assents to whatever is said, merely saying, "It is so."
If someone asks, "How many kinds of aggregates are there?
one should counter-question them:
"How many do you think there are?"
He replied: "In my view, there are five; he said it was so, or else he said that this matter is different, and so forth."
6. The Sixteen Theories of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇavāda). Part Three:
First, the Introduction.
"Furthermore, O good sons among those in samādhi, when their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, Māra finds no opportunity."

If one exhausts the root of all living beings and contemplates that profound, pure source of constant agitation and movement, yet within this inexhaustible flow gives rise to conceptual calculations, such a person falls into the view of post-mortem existence with signs; their initial resolve is inverted.
The "inexhaustible flow" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Now, seeing that formations undergo transition, one instead clings to them as the self.

Regarding those who hold that there is a mark after death: because they consider formations to be what belongs to the self, and since formations flow and shift without ceasing, they conclude that the self exists with a mark after death.
2. Explanation, in two parts:
first, the original thesis.
"Some, being self-attached to the body, say that form is the self."
Or, seeing me as encompassing all lands within my own perfect sphere, they say, "I have form.
Or, when external objects revolve according to me, they say, "Form belongs to me.
Or again, because I am continuous within the midst of conditioned activities, they say, "I am in form."
"All speculate that after death there is a mark; thus, in this cycle, there are sixteen marks.

Initially, four propositions are set forth in full regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), all stating that after death there is a mark; following this cycle, one should apply the same pattern to create twelve propositions for each of the remaining three aggregates.
Regarding "solidifying the body": "solidifying" (*gu*) means "firmness. It refers to firmly grasping the current physical form as one's own fundamental essence.
As it is with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the same applies by analogy to sensation, perception, mental formations, and so forth; thus, sixteen propositions are formed.
Question:

If the first three aggregates have ceased and only the two aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) remain, why would one further cling to the first three, and moreover, why not speak of consciousness?
Answer:

Although the first three aggregates were dismantled during the preceding contemplations, this was merely because the method of observation had become superior, such that one was no longer deluded by the aggregates and could skillfully practice patience without giving rise to afflictions; how could it be said that they were not dismantled at all?

Now, observing the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one perceives it as three because it relies upon and continues the flux of the preceding three aggregates; thus, one clings to them as three.
The reason consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not mentioned is that it is obscured by the aggregate of formations; therefore, it is included within the preceding [three] and not spoken of as consciousness.
2. Distinct Calculations.
"From this, some may calculate that ultimate affliction and ultimate bodhi are two natures that proceed side by side, each remaining untouched by the other."
"Since all sixteen marks exist after death, afflictions are likewise so, for they are the root of birth and death;
and bodhi is likewise so, for it is the luminous source of awakening."
The two—truth and falsehood—are driven apart, yet ultimately there is no change; both possess characteristics.
Third, the conclusion:
"Because of this conceptualization that there is existence after death, one falls into the ways of external paths and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi."
This is called the sixth heterodox teacher, who establishes the inverted view that within the five aggregates there exists a sign of self after death.
Seven and Eight: The Theory of Signlessness; Part Three:
First, the Statement.
"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who maintain a firm, concentrated, and upright mind, Māras cannot find an opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and observe that source of constant agitation within profound stillness. If, while first eliminating form, sensation, and perception, they give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the inverted state of generating the aspiration for enlightenment after death as being signless."

"Having seen that the first three aggregates have already ceased, one should know that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) must likewise cease; thus, one calculates that there is annihilation after death, which is collectively termed 'signlessness' (*animitta*).
2. Explanation, in two parts:
First, the original calculation.
"Seeing that form ceases, one realizes that the physical body has no basis.
Contemplating that perception ceases, one realizes that the mind has no attachments.
Knowing that sensation ceases, one realizes there is no further connection."

The aggregates have dissolved; though the physical form remains, it lacks sensation and perception and is no different from grass or wood. Since this substance cannot even be apprehended while present before you, how could it possess any further characteristics after death?
"By examining and verifying this, one finds that after death there is no mark; thus, in this cycle, there are eight absences of marks.
This refers to the four aggregates: when the present cause perishes and the future fruit ceases, they together constitute these eight.
2. Distinct Calculations.
"From this, some may calculate that nirvana, causes, and effects are all empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to annihilation."
Since the aggregates (*skandhas*) lack both cause and effect, the causes and effects of *nirvāṇa* are likewise entirely extinguished.
Thus, for all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned, defiled or pure—the causes and effects are equally non-existent; therefore, it is said that "all is empty."
3. Conclusion:
"Because they speculate that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the seventh non-Buddhist school, which establishes the inverted doctrine of a mind characterized by the signless state after death within the five aggregates."
8. The Eightfold Argument of Neither-Yes-Nor-No, Part Three:
First, the Statement.
"Furthermore, O virtuous sons within *samādhi*, if you maintain a firm and concentrated upright mind, Māra shall find no opportunity."

Having exhausted the fundamental nature of all living beings, one contemplates that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source; while within the persistence of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), one simultaneously suppresses sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). By dualistically calculating existence and non-existence, one’s own essential nature and its characteristics cancel each other out, and this person falls into the inverted doctrine of "neither existing nor non-existing after death."

"By taking the three aggregates (*skandha*) that have already ceased as an analogy for the currently existing aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one obtains four partial propositions of non-existence (*abhāva*).

Furthermore, by taking the single aggregate of formations that remains as an analogy for the three preceding aggregates that have already ceased, one obtains four partial propositions of non-non-existence (*anabhāva*)."

Viewing the preceding and succeeding moments in relation to one another, each hidden state (陰) attains the status of being neither existent nor non-existent, thereby forming four instances of "neither.
Since it is thus in the present, it is likewise after death.
Together with the present and future, these form eight; therefore, it is said that "after death, all are neither."
2. Explanation, in two parts:
First, the fundamental thesis.

"Within form, sensation, and perception, one perceives both existence and non-existence; within the flux of formations, one contemplates neither existence nor non-existence. Thus cycling through them, one exhausts the aggregates and elements, reaching the eightfold characteristic of 'neither-is-nor-is-not'."
"Whichever condition is encountered, it is all said that after death there is either form (*sanimitta*) or formlessness (*animitta*).

Although the three aggregates (*skandha*), such as form, previously existed, they are now destroyed and exhausted; therefore, it is said they "do not exist. The same principle applies to the others, so these four do not exist.

Regarding the statement that within the internal contemplation of the flux of formations (*saṃskāra*), there is nothing that is not non-existent: if one were to take the aggregate of formations as an example of the preceding [aggregates] and consider them non-existent, they are nonetheless currently undergoing a continuous flux from moment to moment;
thus, they are not non-existent. Since these formations are not non-existent, the same applies to the three preceding aggregates; these four are not non-existent.

Regarding "thus circulating until the aggregates and realms are exhausted": this refers to presently taking the four aggregates as examples and examining them one by one, seeing that each is neither existent nor non-existent; hence, it is called "circulating."
Extending this reasoning to after death, it is said that the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*) are utterly exhausted.
"Whichever condition one encounters" means that among these four aggregates, whichever one is mentioned, all are neither existent nor non-existent after death.
Now, regarding what is called "existence" and "non-existence": existence is not non-existence, and non-existence is not existence.
Second, the separate reckoning:

"Furthermore, because the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and transformation, the mind gives rise to penetrating awakening; both existence and non-existence are negated, and one loses the basis for distinguishing the empty from the real."

"This merely demonstrates that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) undergoes transformation: because there is cessation within arising, it is not existent; because there is arising within cessation, it is not non-existent. By means of this, one universally realizes that all things are neither existent nor non-existent—not merely in these eight cases."
The "empty" and the "real" are simply non-existent. Existence is not fixed as existence; how has the real ever been real?
Non-existence is not fixed as non-existence; how has the empty ever been empty?
Since every instance brought forward is incorrect, it is said that there is no fixed point of reference.
3. Conclusion:

"Because of this speculative reckoning that after death there is neither [existence nor non-existence], and because the future state is shrouded in darkness and beyond description, one falls into the ranks of external paths and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi."
"This is called the eighth heterodox school, which establishes the theory of the inverted mind that after death one is neither [existent nor non-existent] within the five aggregates.
Below the section on the "subsequent limit," the meaning of being "neither" after death is explained.
That which cannot be spoken of means that one cannot say it exists, nor can one say it does not exist; for both paths of existence and non-existence fail to capture the Way.
If this is so even in the present life, how much more so after death, when there is neither perception nor cognition—how then could one speak of existence or non-existence?
Therefore, it is called "obscured and deluded.
Ninth, the doctrine of annihilationism has three parts;
first, the heading.
"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who stabilize their minds with upright concentration, the māras find no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If they subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding non-arising, such persons fall into the seven theories of annihilationism."
This person observes that within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), each moment perishes; this is termed "subsequent non-existence.
Even if one is reborn in seven realms of existence, all such births are ultimately severed and extinguished; thus, this treatise is established.
2. Explanation: "Some reckon on the extinction of the body;

some on the extinction of desire; some on the extinction of suffering; some on the extinction of extreme joy; or some on the extinction of extreme equanimity. Thus, through this cycle, the seven stages of elimination are thoroughly exhausted and manifest as extinguished; once extinguished, they no longer exist."

Some reckon that the cessation of the body refers to humans and devas of the desire realm, as they share the same realm and stage; the exhaustion of desire refers to the first dhyāna; the exhaustion of suffering refers to the second dhyāna; extreme bliss refers to the third dhyāna; and extreme equanimity refers to the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms.
Regarding "extinguished in the present": the three aggregates have already ceased, and the aggregate of formations is likewise.
All seven locations are currently severed and extinguished; after death, one will not be reborn again.
3. Conclusion:
"Because of this reckoning that there is annihilation after death, one falls among the heterodox paths and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the ninth heterodox path: the inverted theory of the mind that establishes the annihilation after death within the five aggregates."
10. The Discourse on the Five Manifestations of Nirvana, in three parts:
First, the introduction.
"Furthermore, O good sons among those in samādhi, when their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, Māra finds no opportunity."

Exhausting the root of all living beings and contemplating that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, those who subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding existence fall into the doctrine of the five nirvāṇas.
Because the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) ceases and then arises again, it is called "subsequent existence" (punarbhava).
Second, the explanation:
"Alternatively, taking the desire realm as the primary basis for transformation (parāvṛtti), one perceives its perfect clarity and thus gives rise to attachment and longing."
Or by means of the first dhyāna, because its nature is free from sorrow;
or by means of the second dhyāna, because the mind is free from suffering;
or by means of the third dhyāna, because it is accompanied by supreme joy.
"Alternatively, by means of the four dhyānas, both suffering and pleasure are extinguished;

because one no longer undergoes the nature of birth and death within saṃsāra, taking the desire realm as the primary basis for transformation (parāvṛtti) means that through the cultivation of contemplative practice, one gives rise to the 'not-yet-attained' concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) of the desire realm. Alternatively, regarding the first dhyāna, it is "without sorrow" because one has already abandoned the defilement of desire; with no further state of mental anxiety and having attained pliancy and bliss, it is so called.
Alternatively, regarding the second dhyāna, it is "without suffering" because this is the state of supreme joy.
Alternatively, that which follows the extreme joy of the third dhyāna is precisely "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
Alternatively, that in which both suffering and pleasure have vanished in the fourth dhyāna is the "feeling of equanimity" (upekṣā-vedanā).

To be deluded regarding these tainted heavens and to take them for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), regarding the security of these five abodes as the supreme pure refuge—thus one revolves through them, taking these five abodes as the ultimate goal.

I. Clarifying the Scope, in two parts:
A. The Characteristics of the Ultimate Perfection of Practice. “Ānanda!

When that good man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is exhausted, the subtle, pure, and turbulent natures of all worldly realms, along with the generative impulses of shared categories, suddenly collapse and fracture. The deep-seated channels through which the *pudgala* repays its karma—the fine and submerged cords—become suspended and severed from their corresponding responses.
The first three phrases identify the person; from "the nature of the world" (*loka-dhātu*) onwards, the text correctly clarifies the exhaustion of formations (*saṃskāra-kṣaya*).
Regarding "the nature of the world": the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is precisely the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the world.
There are two meanings of "world": [the world as a receptacle and the world as sentient beings].
First, they possess arising and ceasing;
second, their nature is tainted;
third, they are subject to destruction.
Having already fallen into the world, they are alike in taking the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as their nature.
It is "profound" because it is hidden; it is "clear" because it is free from conceptualization; and "agitation" is precisely movement.

The preceding section concerning the "equal portion" (*sabhāgatā*) dealt with the fundamental; the present section concerns the essential point of its sudden rupture, hence it is said that it "suddenly falls and splits.
The following passage, beginning with "sinking and becoming subtle," provides a further explanation of the meaning of "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*).
The large ropes on a net are called *gang* (the main lines), and the knotted collars of a garment are called *niu* (buttons); both serve as metaphors for what is essential.

The twelve classes of living beings are like a net or a garment, and the *xing-yin* (aggregate of formations) penetrates through their subtle and minute knots and essentials, acting like the main lines or the buttons.
*Pudgala* (person) is translated as "one who repeatedly takes up existence," which collectively refers to the twelve classes [of beings].

Because the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) can sustain these types of births, it is described as the "subtle net-knot. The "net-knot" refers to the cause—the karma—while *pudgala* refers to the result—the retribution.
If the causal karma perishes, what could lead forth the fruit? If the retribution ceases, who could act as the recipient of the recompense?
Since both cause and effect have vanished, response and resonance are cut off.
"Deep channels" (shenmai) is also a metaphor for the profound obscurity of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
"In the celestial realm of Nirvana, one is about to awaken to the great illumination, like the crowing of a rooster at dawn; looking toward the east, there is already a subtle radiance.
Nirvana is called the "Supreme Celestial Realm" (*paramārtha-deva*), and attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is termed "awakening to the great illumination."
Enlightened realization is near; therefore, it is called "about to" (*jiang*). "About to" means "imminent" or "desiring.
It is like a rooster crowing later: when a rooster crows for the second time, the sky is about to dawn.

The five aggregates remain as they were throughout the entire night; when the aggregates are completely exhausted, it is like the great dawn. When the two aggregates of form and feeling are destroyed, it is like the first crowing of the cock, though the sky has not yet changed at all.

Now that perception and mental formations are further eliminated, only the aggregate of consciousness remains; clear awakening is near, just like the cock’s subsequent crowing when the sky takes on a brilliant hue.
If explained in terms of stages, this refers to the second type of person who progresses gradually. That text states:

"When one is accomplished in the precepts, then within the world there will forever be no karma of mutual birth or mutual killing; theft and robbery will not occur; there will be no mutual indebtedness, nor will one return to repay debts incurred from previous lives."
This refers to the profound mechanism of retribution for karma as presented in the current text, wherein response and resonance are suspended yet absolute.

That text further states: "When these pure persons cultivate samādhi, their physical bodies—parents' fleshly forms—need not rely on the divine eye to naturally perceive the worlds of the ten directions," and so forth.
This text states:
"Looking toward the east, there is already a refined luster. This refers to attaining the stage of semblance, wherein the semblance of supernormal powers (abhijñā) is fully manifested.
Second, the manifestation of signs of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
"The six sense organs are empty and still, no longer wandering or escaping; they are profoundly clear within, entering that which has nothing to enter.

Because they are governed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are no latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); although the six sense organs remain, consciousness does not scatter. Therefore, it is said they are "empty and still, no longer wandering or escaping."
Focusing exclusively on the internal realm, the concentrated mind illuminates within; hence it is said, "internally and internally, profoundly clear.

Furthermore, "internally and internally" refers to a deep, tranquil illumination that reaches the very limit of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate), where nothing further can be perceived; this is called "entering the state of having nowhere to enter."

"Profoundly penetrating the fundamental origins of the twelve types of life-destinies throughout the ten directions, one observes that by grasping their origin, none of these types can summon [rebirth].

The fundamental origin of receiving life is precisely the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate). Now, observing that this *vijñāna-skandha* is the fundamental origin of the seeds for all classes of beings, one does not give rise to afflictions nor create new karma. Because of this sustained restraint, one prevents the arising of karmic fruits; since there is no longer any portion for rebirth, it is said that "none of the various classes can summon [rebirth]."

"Having attained sameness throughout the worlds of the ten directions, its refined essence does not sink, and it reveals what is obscure and secret; this is called the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Since one knows that consciousness is the fundamental source of all living beings, the worlds of the ten directions—both the dependent and the correct—are transformations of consciousness and share the same substance of consciousness. This is what is meant by 'the three realms are mind-only' and 'all phenomena are consciousness-only.'"
Although one previously had faith in the teaching, now one clearly perceives it through direct observation.
That the refined color does not sink means that the object of observation appears; because the power of contemplation causes the objective realm to become clear and distinct, it is said not to sink.
The discovery of what is obscure and secret (*yō-hi*) is like the initial opening [of a door].
Before reaching this stage, the various faculties (*indriya*) are dim and dull, unable to perceive at a distance; therefore, it is called "obscure and secret."

Now, because the six sense organs are purified through the power of contemplation—and not by means of the divine eye (divyacakṣus) that penetrates all realms and so forth—it is said that they "manifest.
Second, the characteristic of exhaustion is explained.

"If, within the stage of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), one has already attained uniformity amidst the collective summons and has refined the six sense-gates, such that their integration and opening are perfected, and seeing and hearing penetrate their neighbors, the mutual functions become pure.
The first two phrases refer to being within the aggregate of consciousness.

If, within this state, one uses the power of concentration and wisdom to grind away the barriers between the sense faculties, causing them to open and merge into a single entity, then seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing will function interchangeably for one another. This is what is meant by "clarity not following the roots," wherein clarity is manifested by relying upon the faculties; therefore, it is said that their mutual functioning is pure.
Having fully realized this consciousness, this is the third gradual stage of realizing the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Thus the text says: "When one who maintains these pure precepts has no mind of greed or lust, they do not flow excessively toward the six external sense objects. Because they do not flow outward, they turn back to their source and return to themselves. When the objects are no longer conditioned, the faculties have nothing to pair with; the flow returns and becomes entirely unified, so that the six functions cease to operate."
Since it is said that "the six functions do not operate," this refers to the subduing and refining of the six gates.
Since it is said that "the flow returns to its entirety as one," this refers to the accomplishment of the unification of opening and closing, wherein the mutual functioning is pure.
That teaching is based on precepts, and thus differs from this one:
"When the worlds of the ten directions, as well as body and mind, become like vaidūrya—transparent and luminous both inside and out—it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness."
"The world, body, and mind are all manifestations of consciousness alone; now that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has been exhausted, there remains only the essence of awakening.
This essence of awakening is luminous and wondrous like pure lapis lazuli, entirely without obstruction, and is termed 'transparency within and without.'"
The body and mind constitute the internal, while the world constitutes the external; since neither can be apprehended, it is called "luminous penetration. As the preceding text states:

"The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, like a precious moon suspended within lapis lazuli. Body and mind are blissful, wondrously perfect, equal, and attain great peace and stability. All the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of all Tathāgatas manifest therein; such a person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
He immediately understood that the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) constitutes partial awakening.
Mañjuśrī also said:
"When rest and renewal are perfected in a single place, the six functions all cease; defilements vanish in a single thought, and perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity is achieved."
"Such a person is then able to transcend the defilement of the lifespan.
When one examines its origin, it is found that its root consists of the formless and void, as well as inverted false imaginings."
The essence of life is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Since life, warmth, and consciousness function simultaneously, once consciousness has departed, life and warmth perish accordingly; thus, one transcends the turbidity of life.

The "phantom-like void" refers to the initial manifestation of images arising from awakened clarity; grasping these deluded thoughts and phantom-like void-images as the substance of consciousness constitutes the two aspects of karmic and transformative phenomena.
